topic: The 1908 Tunguska event: an explosion over Siberia that flattened a forest and left no crater
title: The Explosion That Flattened 80 Million Trees
target_audience: 18-40, curious international viewers of science and history shorts

visual.style: Cinematic stylized 3D: instanced taiga, physically based sky, low sun, long shadows, aerial haze. One warm light per shot (fireball, lantern, low sun) as the ODDLIGHT signature.

scenes.text: In nineteen oh eight, something exploded over Siberia... and flattened eighty million trees.
scenes.visual_goal: Aerial glide over endless taiga before sunrise; a fireball streaks in, lighting the haze and casting moving shadows.

scenes.text: It was early morning. A fireball streaked over the Tunguska river.
scenes.visual_goal: Low river-valley shot; the fireball passes overhead and its light sweeps across trees and water.

scenes.text: Sixty-five kilometres away, a farmer at breakfast saw it all.
scenes.visual_goal: A log homestead at the forest edge, lamp in the window; the horizon flares white.

scenes.text: The blast levelled about two thousand square kilometres of forest.
scenes.visual_goal: High aerial: a dust ring races outward and the trees fall in its path, radially.

scenes.text: The place was so remote, no scientist reached it for nineteen years.
scenes.visual_goal: The flattened forest through passing seasons: snow covers the fallen trunks, light cycles.

scenes.text: When Leonid Kulik finally did, every fallen tree pointed away from one spot.
scenes.visual_goal: Camera rises from an expedition camp lantern to a top-down view of the radial fall pattern.

scenes.text: At the centre, trees still stood... stripped of every branch.
scenes.visual_goal: Ground level among bare upright trunks in mist and low sun; long shadows.
Crane down over the flat bog at ground zero: still water, no hole.

scenes.text: Most likely, a space rock tens of metres wide exploded six to ten kilometres up, with hundreds of times the power of Hiroshima.
scenes.visual_goal: From high above the clouds: a glowing rock enters the atmosphere and bursts high above the forest; altitude marker.

scenes.text: It's still the largest impact in recorded history... and it may never have touched the ground.
scenes.visual_goal: Dusk over the regrown taiga today; the last light collapses into the single ODDLIGHT dot.

footer: Sources: Britannica; NASA Earth Observatory; APS News

claims.text: The explosion happened on the morning of 30 June 1908 over Siberia, near the Podkamennaya Tunguska river.

claims.note: Space.com: more than 80 million trees; Explorersweb gives ~80 million felled or stripped.

claims.text: An eyewitness about 40 miles (~65 km) away saw the event while having breakfast.
claims.note: APS names Sergei Semenov; the narration says 'a farmer' as APS does.

claims.text: About 2,000 square kilometres of forest were flattened.
claims.note: Space.com ~2,000 km2; other sources give 2,150 km2. Narration says 'about'.

claims.text: The first scientific expedition to reach the site was Leonid Kulik's, in 1927 (19 years later).
Kulik found the fallen trees pointing radially away from a central point.
Near the centre, trees were left standing but stripped of their branches.
The leading explanation is the airburst of a space rock (most likely a stony asteroid) tens of metres across.
claims.note: Size estimates vary (~50-80 m in several sources); narration hedges with 'most likely' and 'tens of metres'.

claims.text: The explosion likely occurred about 6-10 km above the surface.
Its energy was hundreds of times that of the Hiroshima bomb.
claims.note: Britannica: up to ~15 Mt, about 1,000x Hiroshima; EarthSky: ~4 Mt, ~250x. 'Hundreds of times' holds across both.

claims.text: Tunguska is the largest impact event in recorded history.
